column1: What are the three primary force modes that arrive at a woodworking joint?
column2: Tension (pulling apart along axis), compression (driving members together in bearing), and shear (sliding one member past another along the glue line/interface).

column1: What is racking, and what causes it?
column2: Racking is the rotational deformation of a rectangular frame into a parallelogram under lateral force; it is not an independent force but a consequence of shear acting at the joint.

column1: Why does a properly executed long-grain edge glue joint typically fail in the wood rather than in the glue line?
column2: Long grain presents open cellulose tubes that modern PVA/aliphatic glues penetrate deeply, curing into a bond stronger in tension/shear than the surrounding wood fiber, so failure occurs in the wood first.

column1: What is the key dimensional invariant for mortise depth relative to tenon width, and why?
column2: Mortise depth should be at least twice the tenon width to provide adequate bearing area for resisting lateral (racking/shear) loads.

column1: What proportion should tenon width be relative to rail thickness, and what general rule sets mortise width relative to the mortised member's thickness?
column2: Tenon width should not exceed one-third of the rail thickness; mortise width is typically set to one-third the thickness of the mortised member.

column1: Mechanically, how do mortise-and-tenon joints resist racking forces?
column2: The tenon cheeks develop shear resistance across glued long-grain surfaces while the tenon shoulders bear in compression against the mortise face, and mortise walls resist lateral movement via bearing stress distributed across mortise depth.

column1: How do dovetail joints structurally differ from mortise-and-tenon joints in the load they resist?
column2: Dovetails use trapezoidal pin/tail geometry to mechanically lock against tensile withdrawal (pull-apart) forces, independent of adhesive, whereas mortise-and-tenon joints primarily resist shear and racking via long-grain bearing/shear surfaces.

column1: Why is wood described as anisotropic, and what is the practical consequence for joinery?
column2: Wood's mechanical properties (strength, stiffness, shrinkage) differ by direction relative to grain—strong and stable along the grain, weak and dimensionally unstable across the grain—so joints must maximize long-grain contact and minimize cross-grain constraints that fight seasonal movement.

column1: Compare tangential and radial shrinkage rates in hardwood like hard maple, and why does this matter for edge-glued panels.
column2: Tangential shrinkage (parallel to growth rings, ~9.5% green-to-oven-dry) is roughly twice radial shrinkage (perpendicular to rings, ~4.8%). Boards with differing ring orientations in a panel move differently, creating permanent internal tension across the glue line even though the glue bond itself is strong.

column1: What problem does a floating panel in a frame-and-panel construction solve, and how?
column2: It accommodates the panel's seasonal cross-grain expansion/contraction by letting the panel float freely in a groove while the surrounding frame maintains its fixed geometry and resists racking.

column1: By what factor does cross-grain dimensional change typically exceed longitudinal (along-grain) expansion in wood?
column2: Roughly a factor of ten to thirty, depending on species and grain orientation—e.g., an 18-inch flat-sawn red oak panel may change width by 3/8 inch seasonally while length stays nearly constant.

column1: What chisel sharpening specification ensures clean fiber severing (rather than crushing) for strong glue bonds in joinery?
column2: A primary bevel of 25 degrees with a 30-degree micro-bevel approximately 0.030 inches wide, honed through 1000 to 6000 grit waterstones to a mirror polish.
